summary:
Tisha Chawla and Susheem Koul of Microsoft present TokenOps, a control plane for FinOps on AI agents. They frame every prior software era as growing a control surface: usage caps in SaaS, autoscaling in cloud, but none in the agentic era at the layer where code invokes a model. Existing tooling (LiteLLM, Portkey, Cloudflare) only hard-caps or downgrades at the request level and cannot intervene in agent loops, sub-agent spawning, or context growth. Their first principles place the token as the unit of cost, attribution at the model-call boundary, and in-place policies (compaction, caching) before a last-resort halt.

TokenOps is an out-of-band plane with three modules: instrumentation (OpenTelemetry, cost in microns), a cumulative accounting ledger, and enforcement via steering and halt actions. On the SDK side, a boundary annotation wraps existing methods to float ledger entries up and channel actions back without code rewrites; a governor enforces the developer-authored list of allowed actions so the control plane cannot arbitrarily mutate behavior; and a wrap_complete helper handles object-based LLM providers. The control plane groups runs into segments by any emitted dimension, sets budgets against a time window, and attaches policies. Two action flavors exist: halt (circuit-breaker kill) and steer (a cost guard that watches budget consumption and velocity, predicting overruns and injecting instructions to keep outputs succinct rather than killing the run).

The live demo uses a two-agent research-and-summarize workflow. Preview mode runs policies with enforcement off; enforcement on demonstrates a halt when a cost cap is exceeded. With the cost guard steering, the run completes under a tighter budget. Benchmarks on browser-use and metagp across stress and scenario tests show average spend falling about 78% with the full policy suite, and the share of completed runs rising from ~67% under simple throttling to ~96% under steering. The supported policy catalog spans spend management, context management (compaction, tool-output reduction), loop detection, and progress detection, with actions of allow, mutate, inject, or kill. The envisioned end state is a self-learning module that reads the ledger to generate new policies or refine existing thresholds to catch remaining runaway costs.

sections.title: From token maxing to value maxing
sections.summary: Tisha introduces the talk, noting AI bills are hard to trace and the industry still celebrates token maxing. She frames the agentic era as lacking a control surface, contrasting SaaS usage caps and cloud autoscaling policies, and motivates the shift to value maxing.

sections.title: Every era got a control surface, this one has not
sections.summary: Tisha argues that gateway-level controls only cap or downgrade at request time and cannot intervene in agent loops, sub-agent spawning, or context growth. She cites news of runaway loops such as Uber exhausting AI budgets in four months and companies spending hundreds of millions in days.

sections.title: First principles at the model call boundary
sections.summary: She lays out first principles - token as unit of cost, attribution at the model-call boundary, and in-place policies (compaction, caching) before a final halt - and positions TokenOps as an out-of-band plane with instrumentation, accounting, and enforcement modules.

sections.title: Why gateways are not enough
sections.summary: She contrasts run-level governance with tools like LiteLLM, Portkey, and Cloudflare that operate at the request level and cannot control loops, context growth, or sub-agent spawning.

sections.title: The SDK side: boundary, ledger, governor
sections.summary: Susheem details the bridge layer: attribution floating dimensions, boundary annotation that tracks I/O as ledger entries and channels actions back, a governor enforcing developer-authorized actions, and wrap_complete for object-based LLM providers. RAG chunk-limiting example is used to illustrate steering.

sections.title: Segments, budgets, actions, policies
sections.summary: On the control plane, he introduces segments built from attributed dimensions, enabling budgets at cohort, agent, or run granularity through rollups.

sections.title: Halt versus steer
sections.summary: Susheem elaborates on budgets as static thresholds over a time window, then contrasts halt (circuit-breaker kill) with steer (in-place behavior adjustment). Policies group budgets and actions against segments or runs. The boundary annotation is out-of-band and the control plane runs in the user's own tenant, with the governor receiving developer-authored configs of allowed actions.

sections.title: Demo: preview mode, then enforcement
sections.summary: Using a two-agent research-and-summarize workflow, the demo runs three scenarios: preview mode (policies evaluate, enforcement off, run completes), enforcement on (cost cap exceeded and agent killed - halt), and cost-guard steering (budget and velocity prediction injects a system instruction to keep outputs succinct, run completes under a tighter budget).

sections.title: Cost guard, and steering on velocity
sections.summary: Susheem explains the cost guard as watching both how much of the allotted budget is consumed and the velocity of token consumption, predicting overruns and injecting instructions such as asking the LLM to keep outputs more succinct or summarized.

sections.title: Benchmark results and the policy catalog
sections.summary: Benchmarks on browser-use and metagp across stress and scenario tests show ~78% average spend reduction with the full policy suite, and completion rising from ~67% under throttling to ~96% under steering. The policy catalog covers spend management, context compaction, tool-output reduction, loop detection, and progress detection, with allow/mutate/inject and kill actions.

sections.title: A self learning control plane
sections.summary: Susheem describes the envisioned self-learning module that reads the continuously updated ledger to detect missing failure modes, then either generates new policies on the fly or refines existing thresholds to manage runaway costs more effectively. He closes with a QR code to the public wiki and an invitation for questions.

demonstrations: Live two-agent research-and-summarize workflow: preview mode (policies evaluate, enforcement off), enforcement on triggering a halt on budget exceedance, and cost-guard steering producing a succinct system-instruction injection to fit a tighter budget.
Walkthrough of boundary annotation applied to a RAG retrieval tool returning 20 chunks, with the control plane pushing a steer action to limit output to the top 5 relevant chunks.
Dashboard view of governance output showing policies (cost budget, cost guard) executing with governance toggled on and off.
limitations: Existing model gateways (LiteLLM, Portkey, Cloudflare) only hard-cap or downgrade at the request level and cannot control agent loops, sub-agent spawning, or context growth.
Simple throttling cuts bills by killing runs, leaving completion rates low (67%).
The self-learning policy generation module is described as an envisioned end state, not yet delivered.
quantitativeClaims: Benchmarked average spend reduction of about 78% with TokenOps' full policy suite on browser-use and metagp.
Completion rate rose from ~67% under simple throttling to ~96% under steering on those benchmarks.
Uber reportedly exhausted its AI budget within 4 months.
Some companies reportedly spent hundreds of millions of dollars in days due to runaway loops.
